title: Donor Variability and Stromal Vascular Fraction Isolation Outcomes: Implications for Adipose Tissue-Derived ATMP Manufacturing
content: Stromal vascular fraction (SVF) isolated from adipose tissue is an important source of starting material for adipose tissue-derived advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), but the influence of donor-related and harvesting-related factors on SVF isolation outcomes remains unclear. In this study, SVF was isolated from adipose tissue samples obtained from 100 adult donors undergoing elective liposuction using a standardized enzymatic digestion protocol. Donor age, body mass index (BMI), waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), and harvesting site were evaluated in relation to SVF yield, isolation efficiency, and cell viability using correlation and non-parametric statistical analyses. SVF was successfully isolated from all samples. Mean SVF yield was 16.7 ± 9.68 × 10⁶ cells per 100 mL of adipose tissue, and mean viability was 80.9 ± 9.97%. No significant associations were observed between donor age and SVF yield, isolation efficiency, or viability. Similarly, BMI and WHR were not significantly associated with SVF isolation outcomes, although BMI showed a weak positive trend with isolation efficiency (ρ = 0.181, p = 0.086). Harvesting site had no significant effect on isolation outcomes despite numerically higher yield and viability in thigh-derived samples. Initial SVF viability was not associated with subsequent ADSC yield or viability after culture. Overall, demographic, anthropometric, and harvesting-site characteristics showed limited influence on quantitative SVF isolation outcomes. These findings support the robustness of standardized SVF isolation procedures and indicate that adipose tissue represents a reliable source of starting material for adipose tissue-derived ATMP manufacturing.
